The term “AI slop” hides conversations we need to have. When we call something “AI slop,” we’re often doing more than complaining about one output. Optimists use the term to quarantine failures away from AI’s promise; critics use it to indict the whole technology. Slop-talk thus lets us feel like we’re discussing important social issues without actually doing it. I argue that we should have those discussions openly.

This spring, arXiv started banning authors whose submissions bear the marks of unchecked AI use, the latest of several key institutions to move against “AI slop 1 , 2 .” The reactions make sense, since cheap synthetic text now floods not only research repositories but also traditional and social media, art, advertisements, and even legal briefs. But what worries me is less the slop itself than how we’re using the term. Sometimes we use the term just to complain about a bad AI output, but often we use it to smuggle in one of two much broader views about AI’s proper role in society, taking sides in an important social debate while seeming only to sneer at a single output. The move is slippery, often unintentional, and it allows us to avoid important discussions we should be having.

One attitude “AI slop” can express is an attitude of quarantine. In this use, the slop is seen as unfortunate and not representative. To call it “slop” is to try to cordon it off from the good stuff that AI can produce, the useful translation, the genuinely helpful code, or the new mathematical discovery 3 . This is how Sam Altman used the term when OpenAI launched Sora 2. Creativity, he wrote, could be headed for “a Cambrian explosion,” while the “RL-optimized slop feed” was a degenerate case they put great care into avoiding 4 . It is also the attitude Google tried to take when its AI search suggested using glue to keep cheese on pizza. The company said such results came from uncommon queries 5 . The embarrassing case was sealed off so the rollout could go on.

A second attitude is one of contagion. In this use, the slop is not a defective specimen but a revelation. The bad output shows us what AI really is, a technology inherently derivative, careless, and hostile to the culture it feeds on. The critic says, look at the synthetic children’s books, the student essays no one wrote, and the apology emails no one stands behind. Those aren’t unfortunate by-products but perfect representatives of what AI can do for us. This is the move Madsen and Puyt make 6 , treating the flood of derivative, recycled output not as a defect to be cleaned up but as what AI amounts to. And it is how the Atlantic ’s Charlie Warzel answered Sora 2’s launch three weeks later. “AI slop is winning,” the piece announced, and what Altman was describing was “a world of creativity without craft 7 .”

There’s something commendable in both attitudes. The quarantine attitude rightly reminds us that not every AI system or output is the same. The contagion attitude reminds us to be on the lookout for slop, since many incentives reward cheap, low-value production. My concern is not with either attitude but with how the term lets us avoid saying which way we intend it. In the optimist’s mind it is only slop, with the emphasis falling on the “slop”; in the critic’s mind it is all slop, with the emphasis falling on the “AI.” And importantly, two people on opposite sides of the bigger social questions can walk away from a discussion thinking they agree because they’ve settled that some output is AI slop, when really the larger disagreement was hidden by their differing intentions in using the term.

The trick is that “AI slop” presents itself as a verdict on an output while implicitly suggesting a verdict on the technology 8 , 9 , the same move behind the charge that a text “sounds like AI 10 .” Beyond calling an output cheap and low-value, it invites disgust and suggests we recoil (philosophers of language would call it a “thick” term, one that describes and evaluates at once). That recoil can mean two different things. In the optimist’s mouth, it’s a push to quarantine the output from AI’s valuable work; in the critic’s mouth, it’s a push to scuttle the whole enterprise. But disgust at a particular output is one thing, and a verdict on the whole category is another, and the term lets us slide from the first to the second without noticing.

We can see that this slide is a cheat by recalling that there was slop long before there was AI 11 . There were bad novels, formulaic films, empty lectures, and academic committee reports that said nothing at length. But no one thought that bad novels settled the worth of literature or that a worthless report settled whether academia should keep committees. This point cuts both ways. The slop coming out of our machines doesn’t show that AI is worthless any more than its good outputs show that it’s good on the whole. So when discussions of “AI slop” seem to bear on this, it must be some background view about AI’s proper role that’s really doing the work. It’s that background view we really need to be discussing, and when we get there via “AI slop,” it’s typically carried in quietly and left undefended.

None of this is to say that there’s nothing unique about AI slop. AI does change the scale, speed, and cost of producing low-value outputs, and makes some of them harder to spot, more profitable to spread, and more apt to poison the data future models learn from 12 . Those are real worries, but they are worries about how the technology is designed, owned, deployed, and used. They are not proof of its overall value or worthlessness.

The natural contrast with slop is quality, and often quality is all that is at issue. Ask whether a particular manuscript is slop and you are usually just asking whether it is any good, and that may be all an editor needs to know. But quality is not a stance on how we should live. The better AI gets, the more tempting it is to think the quality settles something bigger. It doesn’t. A machine can write a flawless condolence note, and whether such a note ought to be machine-written is left exactly where it was. Quality answers the easy question and stays silent on the hard one.

So instead of focusing on AI slop, we should ask directly the questions slop-talk lets us postpone by seeming to settle them, questions about the kind of society we should be building and what roles AI should play in it. When someone is sick, lonely, or frightened, do we want a real person in the room, or will a bot do? 13 Do we want our children taught and shaped mostly by people, or are we content to hand that to machines? When a court weighs whom to believe, or an employer whom to hire, do we want a person behind the call, or can a machine sort it? 14 Do we want the systems that increasingly run our lives steered by a few private companies, or held more widely accountable? And do we want a shared world we can make sense of together, or one so flooded with synthetic stuff that no one can tell what is real? 15 None of these can be answered by asking whether AI produces quality or slop. They are about the communal lives we want, and when we reach for “AI slop,” we’re sloppily pushing each other on exactly these questions without ever confronting them out loud.

I am not saying we should ban the term “AI slop.” Sometimes we want to name what should be shovelled into the trough, and that term will do. But we should stop letting it stand in for the tough collective discussions we should be having. There are small ways to start. When we reach for “AI slop,” we can try to be explicit about whether we mean to give a verdict on an output or a verdict on the technology. And our institutions can say, when they ban slop, what they are and are not deciding.

Consider arXiv again. To its credit, the rule it implemented is narrower than the headlines suggested. Announcing it, the chair of arXiv’s computer-science section clarified that the rule is only about the quality of the submitted piece, writing that when a submission shows “incontrovertible evidence that the authors did not check the results of LLM generation,” the upshot is that “we can’t trust anything in the paper 16 .” But to my bigger point, the ban was read as a stand anyway. One commentator cheered it as a blow against “the slop machine,” 17 while another countered that AI-generated text “is not a problem in itself” and that the answer to the flood of slop may be “more AI, not less 18 .” So while a policy can keep to the quality question, the term drags the bigger issues in, and it gets used in the two different ways without the difference ever being marked. That is exactly why saying what you do and do not mean by the term matters, and when others reach for the term, we should ask what they mean as well. This is how we’ll make progress on tackling those bigger societal questions about how much of our shared lives we want to turn over to the technology and how much we want to keep for ourselves.
